messages.content:
Write the postmortem for the incident below.

Alert: HighErrorRate on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: Error rate above threshold for 5m {A1}
Alert raised: 2026-10-25T22:08:00Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged.
The alert rule waits 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires: that wait is part of the time from the onset to the alert - count it before calling detection slow. The alert came 1 minute {after_the_wait} after that wait ended. Its condition looks back over 1 minute {rule_looks_back}: up to that much of the time from the onset to the alert is that window filling - count it before calling detection slow.
Broken from 2026-10-25T22:02:00Z {began} (the onset) to 2026-10-25T22:09:00Z {back_to_normal}, when the metrics show it back to normal.
That is 7 minutes {duration}, and every impact figure below is measured over that stretch.
Argus held the incident for 1 minute 59 seconds {held}, until 2026-10-25T22:10:02Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
Error rate before it began: 1.0% {errors_before}.
Error rate while it was broken: 29.1% {errors_while_broken}, peaking at 37.0% {errors_at_worst}.
Rise above baseline: 28.1% {errors_rise} of traffic failed that otherwise would not have.
The series behind the alert, `sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[1m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[1m]))` - its alert said "Error rate above threshold for 5m {A1}" - which its alert rule evaluates and calls worse rising: 1.0166666666666666% {series_before} before it began, 29.14285714285714% {series_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and 37% {series_at_worst} at its worst. Say what it measures in words, not by its query.
Customer loss: 4,474.52 USD {customer_loss} - how far the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier, beyond how much those hours vary on their own.

What Argus did, in order:
  - [T1] 2026-10-25T22:08:02Z {T1.1} Argus: Received HighErrorRate on io-shop
  - [T2] 2026-10-25T22:08:03Z {T2.1} Argus: Moved the incident to INVESTIGATING - a worker took the incident up
  - [T3] 2026-10-25T22:08:03Z {T3.1} Argus: Called in the Investigator Agent
  - [T4] 2026-10-25T22:08:04Z {T4.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for the service's per-minute metrics, anchored on 22:08 {T4.2}
  - [T5] 2026-10-25T22:08:04Z {T5.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 361 {T5.2} minutes of metrics
  - [T6] 2026-10-25T22:08:04Z {T6.1} Investigator Agent: Placed the start of the incident at 22:02 {T6.2}
  - [T7] 2026-10-25T22:08:04Z {T7.1} Investigator Agent: Recorded where the 3 {T7.2} replicas run - all on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB
  - [T8] 2026-10-25T22:08:07Z {T8.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 1 {T8.2} day before Oct 25 22:02 {T8.3}
  - [T9] 2026-10-25T22:08:08Z {T9.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 1 {T9.2} production change
  - [T10] 2026-10-25T22:08:08Z {T10.1} Investigator Agent: Read how far the deployment had rolled out - all 3 {T10.2} replicas run one revision, which the history does not name
  - [T11] 2026-10-25T22:08:08Z {T11.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for the service's log lines, the 36 {T11.2} minutes before 22:08 {T11.3}
  - [T12] 2026-10-25T22:08:08Z {T12.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 133 {T12.2} log lines
  - [T13] 2026-10-25T22:08:12Z {T13.1} Investigator Agent: Formed 1 {T13.2} candidate cause, best first: C1
  - [T14] 2026-10-25T22:08:12Z {T14.1} Investigator Agent: Read every channel available
  - [T15] 2026-10-25T22:08:12Z {T15.1} Argus: Read the flag provider's history - 1 {T15.2} flag change by anyone but Argus, the 1 {T15.3} hour before 22:08:12 {T15.4}
  - [T16] 2026-10-25T22:08:13Z {T16.1} Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATING to act on the leading candidate
  - [T17] 2026-10-25T22:08:13Z {T17.1} Argus: Called in the Mitigation Agent
  - [T18] 2026-10-25T22:08:13Z {T18.1} Mitigation Agent: Reverted the feature flag monthly-spend-feature, moved from ON to OFF
  - [T19] 2026-10-25T22:08:16Z {T19.1} Mitigation Agent: Waiting to see whether the service is still at the incident's level, from 22:09 {T19.2} - up to 120s {T19.3}
  - [T20] 2026-10-25T22:10:02Z {T20.1} Mitigation Agent: Looked at the service - no longer at the incident's level since 22:09 {T20.2}
  - [T21] 2026-10-25T22:10:02Z {T21.1} Mitigation Agent: Judged the action CONFIRMED
  - [T22] 2026-10-25T22:10:02Z {T22.1} Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATED - set flag [monthly-spend-feature] OFF and the rule that fired stopped firing
  - [T23] 2026-10-25T22:10:48Z {T23.1} Code-Fix Agent: Proposed a fix as a draft pull request - https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/351

Changes to production it read:
  - [P1] 2026-10-25T22:02:00Z {P1.1} flag-toggle monthly-spend-feature by admin: feature flag monthly-spend-feature was switched on
  - Deploys read, none came back.

Log lines it read, one per message:
  - [G7e5d] INFO io-shop: monthly-spend-feature=off - 200 {G7e5d.1} evaluations - 30 {G7e5d.2} occurrences in 30 {G7e5d.3} minutes, 21:32–22:01 {G7e5d.4}
  - [G46bc] ERROR io-shop: account page request failed - ClientDisconnected: the shopper closed the connection - 46 {G46bc.1} occurrences in 37 {G46bc.2} minutes, 21:32–22:08 {G46bc.3}
  - [Gbac1] WARN io-shop: account page error rate at #% over the last minute - 33 {Gbac1.1} occurrences in 37 {Gbac1.2} minutes, 21:32–22:08 {Gbac1.3}; # was 0.50 {Gbac1.4} to 37.00 {Gbac1.5}, typically 1.50 {Gbac1.6}, highest at 22:05 {Gbac1.7}
  - [Gad41] INFO io-shop: account pages rendered normally - 4 {Gad41.1} occurrences in 8 {Gad41.2} minutes, 21:53–22:00 {Gad41.3}
  - [G971b] 22:02 {G971b.1} INFO io-shop: monthly-spend-feature=off 29 {G971b.2} / on 171 {G971b.3} - 200 {G971b.4} evaluations
  - [G5309] ERROR io-shop: account page request failed - ZeroDivisionError: division by zero at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47 - 13 {G5309.1} occurrences in 7 {G5309.2} minutes, 22:02–22:08 {G5309.3}
  - [Gce95] INFO io-shop: monthly-spend-feature=on - 200 {Gce95.1} evaluations - 6 {Gce95.2} occurrences in 6 {Gce95.3} minutes, 22:03–22:08 {Gce95.4}

Candidates it considered, in the Investigator's words - cite them; what they claim is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [C1] The feature flag monthly-spend-feature was switched on at 2026-10-25T22:02:00Z {C1.1}. Account page requests that take the new spend-summary path now fail with ZeroDivisionError at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47, and the error rate stepped from about 1% {C1.2} to about 30% {C1.3}. No deployment landed and the replicas are on one revision. [feature-flag-toggle, confidence 0.93 {C1.4}, confirmed]

Actions it took:
  - [M1] Reverted the feature flag monthly-spend-feature (can be put back) - confirmed, still in place

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] The fault: in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py, `average_spend_per_item_this_month` builds the list of this month's purchases and returns `account.total_this_month_cents // len(bought_this_month)`. A shopper who has bought before but not this month has an empty list, so that line divides by zero (line 47 {F1.1}, as the evidence shows). The lifetime average has a similar divisor, but it is only empty for an account that has never bought anything. The monthly divisor is empty for an ordinary shopper who just hasn't bought yet this month, and that is very common. Turning on monthly-spend-feature sent those requests down this path. `serve_account_page` in src/io_shop/account_page.py catches the exception at the request boundary and turns it into a failed page, which is why the error rate jumped.
      
      The fix: when nothing was bought this month, `average_spend_per_item_this_month` now returns 0 {F1.2} and does not divide. Zero is the true figure for a month with no spending, and it keeps the function's `int` return type. Its callers (`render_spend_summary`, and through it `_the_figure_for` in account_page.py) render whatever int comes back, so they need no change. With the flag on, those shoppers now see a page rather than an error. With the flag off, nothing changes. The lifetime average is untouched, and so is the existing test that expects a never-bought account to raise there. Nothing is swallowed: an empty month is handled as a valid input, not by catching an exception.
      
      The tests: the new cases in tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py call `average_spend_per_item_this_month` directly, and `render_spend_summary` with use_monthly_summary=True, on a shopper who has past purchases but none this month, and assert the result is 0 {F1.3}. Against the current code both calls raise ZeroDivisionError. Nothing has run these tests yet.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'.

Action items the record already holds:
  - AI-1 (mitigate, done): Reverted the feature flag monthly-spend-feature
  - AI-2 (prevent, open): Review and merge the proposed fix
PR #351 is a draft Argus opened for a person to review and merge. The record holds nothing about it after that: do not say it was reviewed, approved or merged, or that it was not - nor that the record holds nothing, which the document says itself. Nothing ran its test or its fix: say what it proposes, not that it corrects anything.
The document already states what set it off, in a section of its own: the change [P1].

Cite evidence in causal_chain by its label. In a contributing factor's addressed_by, name the record's own action items that answer it, by their number; an item you propose names the factors it answers in its answers, by their labels.

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

action_items.item: Turn on monthly-spend-feature, and flags like it, in stages, starting with a small share of shoppers instead of most traffic at once.
Watch the account page error rate at each stage of a flag rollout, and switch the flag back off automatically when the rate rises above its baseline.
Require tests that exercise a flag's on path before the flag can be switched on in production, including accounts with past purchases but none this month.
Keep monthly-spend-feature off until the fix proposed in pull request #351 has been merged and deployed.
Route HighErrorRate on io-shop so that it pages the on-call engineer.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account page requests failed. The share of all requests returning server errors rose from {series_before} before the onset to {series_while_broken} on average, with a peak of {series_at_worst}. The service's own warning put the account page error rate at its highest at {Gbac1.7}.
From {G5309.3}, account page requests raised ZeroDivisionError: division by zero in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py, at line {F1.1}, and each one became a failed page.

ruled_out.what: A deployment: no deploy came back for the day before the onset, the only production change read was the flag switch, and all replicas run one revision.

Shoppers closing the connection (ClientDisconnected): these errors show up across the whole log window, including before the onset, while the account page error rate sat near its usual level and pages rendered normally.

causal_chain.step: Requests reached that code because the feature flag monthly-spend-feature was switched on by admin at {P1.1}. That sent account page requests down the new spend-summary path. Before the switch, every flag evaluation came back off. In the minute of the switch, {G971b.3} of {G971b.4} came back on, and after that every evaluation came back on. Switching the flag off at {T18.1} brought the service back below the incident's level from {T20.2}, and the action was judged confirmed.

The division by zero likely happens because the monthly average divides by the number of this month's purchases. That list is empty for an ordinary shopper who has bought before but not yet this month, which Code-Fix's reading calls very common. The lifetime average's divisor is empty only for accounts that have never bought anything.

input.cause_in_plain_words: Switching on a new monthly spending summary sent shoppers' account pages through a calculation that divided by zero, likely because shoppers who had bought before but not yet this month had no purchases this month to divide by.

contributing_factors.factor: No test of the flag-on spend-summary path for a shopper with past purchases but none this month was seen before the flag was switched on. Code-Fix's reading says such calls raise ZeroDivisionError against the current code.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A test like that would have hit the division by zero before the flag was switched on in production.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: The flag went from off to on for most evaluations in one step. In the first minute, {G971b.3} of {G971b.4} evaluations were on, and every evaluation was on after that. No staged rollout of the flag was seen, and no check of the error rate tied to the flag change was seen.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A staged rollout would have exposed only a small share of shoppers to the failing path, and a check tied to the flag change could have switched it back before most traffic was hit.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

went_well: Argus switched monthly-spend-feature off {T18.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised, acting on the only candidate, and the revert can be undone.
Argus confirmed the revert from the service's own metrics before marking the incident mitigated.
Code-Fix opened draft pull request #351 {T23.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised, with tests for shoppers who have past purchases but none this month.
went_wrong: Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked, so no person was told about an incident in which a large share of account pages failed.

input.root_cause: With monthly-spend-feature on, account pages go through `average_spend_per_item_this_month` in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. That function divides the shopper's total for this month by the number of purchases they made this month. For a shopper who has bought before but not yet this month, that number is zero, so the request raised ZeroDivisionError at line {F1.1}. `serve_account_page` caught the error at the request boundary and returned a failed page.
input.still_at_risk: The division by zero is still in the code with the flag off, so switching monthly-spend-feature back on would likely make account pages fail again for shoppers who have bought before but not yet this month.
input.symptom: Account pages failed to load for many shoppers

content.content:
Your postmortem was not accepted:
  - your answer writes [From {G5309.3}] - [{G5309.3}] is a range and says its own: write it alone, or say over or during

Call submit_postmortem again with the whole answer, corrected.

system.text:
You write the postmortem for an incident Argus has already handled. One message describes it - what Argus did and read, the candidate causes, the actions and what they came to, and every figure already measured - and you answer by calling submit_postmortem. Nothing is left to look up.

The candidates are the Investigator's account, written while the incident ran and before anything was tried. The record - the lines saying what Argus did, the changes, the log lines, the actions and their verdicts - is what happened. Where the two disagree, the record is right.

Write causal_chain as the five whys. The first step is the symptom: what the people using the service saw, with the evidence that shows it. The symptom field is that step in a few words, and the two must agree. Each step after it answers why the step before happened - one cause, no jumps - and cites its evidence from the record, never a candidate: a candidate is a hypothesis, and the chain says what happened. Five is a guide, not a quota: stop where the evidence stops. The root_cause field says the mechanism: the step of the chain that says why the change broke the service.

A why the record cannot answer - a missing test, a missing safeguard, an alert that came late - is a contributing factor rather than a step, and each contributing factor names an action item that answers it. Where one why has several answers, follow the one that leads to the fault and make the others contributing factors.

Never stop at a person. Where somebody's action set the incident off, ask why the system let that action do harm - why it was possible at all - and carry on from there.

tools.description: Submit the postmortem for this incident. Every field is required. Write no figure yourself anywhere in your answer - no time, duration, percentage, count or amount, not in digits and not spelled out in words. Every figure you are shown is followed by its name in braces, like {A3} or {duration}: where your prose states one, write its name, braces and all, and the document writes the figure in. A figure you were not shown but could work out from two you were - the span between two instants, how far one share is above another, how many times one is the other - is written as that working, braces and all: {back_to_normal - began}, {T3.1 - alert_raised}, {errors_at_worst / errors_before}. The document works it out from the figures as you were shown them. Say any other size with no number in it, not even in a word - "most requests", "for several minutes", never "twenty minutes", "a third" or "tripled". A number is a figure even with a unit or a clock's marks on it (5m, 10ms, 3x, 12:05Z). Any other word with a digit in it is a name - a label you cite (T2, G3fa2, C1, AI-1), a version (v2), a revision, a pod - and is written as given. State only what the evidence you are shown says: where the record does not show something - a check that was or was not run, how many replicas - leave it out or say it was not seen.

action_items.description: What should be done that the record does not already hold, each one thing a person could take on: two things to do are two items. Empty where the record's own items answer every factor. Propose nothing to confirm a cause the record already confirmed - a mitigation that worked, a hypothesis marked confirmed - and no check of what the evidence you are shown already shows: a diff states what changed. Where an F row says to check something a D row shows, say what the D row shows, and the item is what follows from it.

answers.description: The labels of the contributing factors it answers: CF-1. Empty where it answers none.

assumptions.description: Anything else the reader should know was assumed rather than measured. Empty is a valid answer.

causal_chain.description: The cause as the five whys, from the symptom down: the first step is what users saw - or, where nobody using the service saw anything wrong, that and what was seen instead - and each step after it answers why the step directly before it happened. The first why says why the symptom happened, not the symptom again in more detail. Where the incident needed two things at once - something going wrong, and nothing in place to contain it - follow the one that leads to what set it off; the other is one of the contributing_factors, not named in the chain. A safeguard that did not stop it is never a step of its own: it is one of the contributing_factors. Every step cites at least one piece of evidence by its label. Date a change by its own row's instant - the T or P row that records it - never by an effect it had. A state a row read - how many replicas run a revision, which way a flag is set - is known as of the row that read it, by that row's instant, which is its first figure, as T3.1 is T3's - not from when the change was made. What else the record ruled out - an earlier change, a flag the provider showed unchanged, a candidate refuted - goes in the ruled_out of the step that ties the incident to the change that set it off, citing what ruled it out, and never as a step. An earlier change is ruled out only by the service measured healthy with it in place - in metrics read between it and the onset, in an alert that dates the first harm itself at or after a later change (at, where the two instants are the same), or after a confirmed action that left it there - never by how long before the onset it came. Where the record shows none of these, it was not ruled out: say so in that step itself. Stop where the evidence stops.

cites.description: The labels of the evidence that shows this step: T3, G3fa2. Not rows that merely happened at the same time.

ruled_out.description: What else the record ruled out at this step, each what it was and why. Empty on every step but the one that ties the incident to the change that set it off.

cites.description: The labels of what ruled it out.

cause_in_plain_words.description: What caused the incident, in one sentence for a reader who does not work on the service: no component names unless they are unavoidable. When it began, for how long, how bad it got, what customers lost and what was done the document says itself - say none of them. Say only what the record says - of a change, of the service, of the people - and nothing it does not. Where part of it rests only on a reading nothing ran, say that part as likely, in plain words, without mentioning the reading.

cause_rests_on_an_unrun_reading.description: Whether the mechanism in root_cause rests on an F row - a reading of the code nothing ran - with no S or D row showing what it rests on. Where you answer true, the document says itself, beside the root cause, that the cause is unverified, and leaves its root-cause review box for a person: say neither in root_cause.

contributing_factors.description: Conditions that had to hold for the incident to happen and did not cause it alone - a safeguard that did not stop it, a gap in detection or review. A factor held before the incident began: what the response did, declined or left behind - an action taken or not, automatic sync left off - is not one; where it went wrong, say it under went_wrong. Not the root cause again in other words: a factor is something that, had it been otherwise, would have stopped or shortened the incident even with what root_cause says still true. A safeguard the record does not show is one not seen, never one absent: write that no check was seen, not that none ran. An alert finds what its rule watches, not the cause behind it: say a fault was found only by what the record shows found it. Each is answered by at least one action item: one of the record's, named in its addressed_by, or one you propose, whose answers name it.

addressed_by.description: The record's own action items that answer it, by the numbers the record gives them: AI-1. Empty where none of them does. Never an item you propose: that item names, in its own answers, the factors it answers.

had_it_been_otherwise.description: What would have gone differently had this been otherwise - stopped, shortened or caught sooner - with what root_cause says still true. A factor that only says the root cause again cannot answer this: leave it out of the list.

label.description: CF-1 for the first factor, CF-2 for the next, and so on in the order you give them. Written here and in an item's answers, never in your prose: the reader never sees it.

lessons.description: What went well, what went wrong, and where the incident got lucky - a risk that went unnoticed this time. Any list may be empty. A safeguard the record does not show is one not seen, never one absent: write that no check was seen, not that none ran. How soon the alert came is weighed by the document already, from what was measured: say nothing of it here.

got_lucky.description: Something the record shows went the fortunate way by chance, and would have made it worse had it not. Empty where the record shows none. Not what kind of fault it was, which the impact already says, nor a limit of what the record shows, which is said in assumptions as what was assumed.

went_well.description: Where one says how quickly Argus did something, write the span as a working of two instants - a T or P row's instant is its first figure, as T3.1 is T3's: {T3.1 - alert_raised}, not in words ("within seconds"). Set the span beside what it times - the thing its later instant dates - not after something else in the same sentence. Name what Code-Fix proposed without saying what it does: the action items and Code-Fix's own reading say that, with its conditions.

went_wrong.description: A change the response left in place on purpose, which one of the record's own action items undoes (automatic sync left off), went as designed and did not go wrong; so did what the design leaves to a person - a draft fix to review and merge. Not a limit of what the record shows - logs nobody read, metrics that stop short of the onset: the document says what was read, and anything assumed is said in assumptions. Not the root cause or a contributing factor again - the document says those already.

reaches_a_cause.description: Whether the chain says why the change that set the incident off broke the service, rather than stopping at that change. A step resting on F rows - a reading of the code nothing ran - counts: whether that leaves the cause unverified is cause_rests_on_an_unrun_reading's to say. That a new version does worse is what the change did, not why it broke the service: answer false where the chain says the evidence does not show why.

root_cause.description: What caused the incident, in one or two sentences, written for an engineer who was not on the call: the mechanism - why the change that set it off broke the service, as far as the evidence goes, a missing protection or not. Not the trigger, how it was confirmed, what resolved it or what was ruled out - the document states each of those itself. Not one of the contributing_factors: a safeguard that would have stopped it with this mechanism unchanged is said there, not here. What the service did over the stretch the metrics did not watch is not the mechanism: the document says it itself. Whether it was verified the document says itself, from your answer to cause_rests_on_an_unrun_reading - do not say it.

still_at_risk.description: What was still at risk at the end of the time Argus held the incident, in one sentence for the same reader - what the fault still in place then could yet do, or the same thing able to happen again. Empty where nothing was. Not whether the service or its metrics were back, nor why - the summary says both. Not what Argus left to a person - a draft fix, automatic sync left off, a recommended action - which the document says itself. Say only what the record says: nothing of the service after that was read.

symptom.description: What went wrong as somebody using the service saw it, as short as it can be: it is the document's title. One sentence with no number in it, never over 16 words - the thing that went wrong and what happened to it, with an active verb: 'Account pages failed'. Not the metric the alert fired on, not the cause - the document adds the change it began with itself - and not how it was found, which the document's Detection says. Where nobody using the service saw anything wrong, say that and what was seen instead, in that one sentence.

tools.name: submit_postmortem
